head: 'Kenton' probably means the farm of a man called Coena.
text: It ends in Old English tūn, a farm or settlement. South Kenton station opened in 1933 for new houses.

head: Named after the quays of the South Dock of the West India Docks.
text: The docks opened in the early 19th century. The quays are now lined with office towers.

head: Named after Ruislip, the leaping place where rushes grow.
text: The station opened in 1908 as Northolt Junction and only became South Ruislip in 1947. The Central line arrived in 1948.

head: 'Tottenham' means the homestead of a man called Totta.
text: It is in the Domesday Book of 1086 as Toteham. South Tottenham station opened in 1871.

head: Named after Wimbledon, though the station is actually in Merton.
text: 'Wimbledon' probably means the hill of a man called Wynnmann. For many years the station was called South Wimbledon (Merton) to make this clear.

head: 'Woodford' means the ford by the wood.
text: The ford crossed the River Roding. The station opened in 1856 as George Lane, after the road outside, and its name changed several times before settling as South Woodford.

head: 'Southall' means the southern nook of land.
text: It comes from Old English sūth and healh, a corner or nook; its partner to the north is Northolt. Southall has a large Punjabi community, and the station signs are also written in Punjabi.

head: Named after Southbury Road, from an old name for the southern part of Enfield.
text: '-bury' usually means a manor. The station opened in 1891 as Churchbury, closed in 1909, and reopened as Southbury in 1960.

head: Named after the south fields of Wandsworth, open farmland for centuries.
text: They were first recorded in the 13th century and stayed fields until about 1900. During the Wimbledon tennis championships, this is the station for the courts.

head: Named after the south gate into Enfield Chase, a royal hunting ground.
text: The village grew up around the gate. The round station of 1933, designed by Charles Holden, is listed as a historic building.

head: 'Southwark' means the southern fort.
text: It was recorded in the early 10th century as Suthriganaweorc, the fort of the men of Surrey, defending the southern end of London Bridge. The station opened in 1999.

head: Named after St James Street in Walthamstow.
text: The street takes its name from St James's Church, built in the 19th century for the growing town. Walthamstow means the place of welcome.

head: Named after St James's Park, which takes its name from St James's Palace.
text: The palace was built by Henry VIII on the site of a medieval hospital for women with leprosy, dedicated to St James the Less. The park is the oldest of London's royal parks.

head: Named after the Knights of St John, who owned the woods here.
text: The Order of St John of Jerusalem had its priory in Clerkenwell and held this wooded land in the Middle Ages. The station opened in 1939.

head: Named after St Paul's Cathedral, just to the south.
text: There has been a church dedicated to St Paul on this hill since 604. The station opened in 1900 as Post Office, after the head office of the Post Office nearby, and was renamed in 1937.

head: Named after a stream, now lost, between Hammersmith and Chiswick.
text: 'Stamford' is said to mean the stony ford. The brook now runs in a pipe under the streets.

head: 'Stamford' means the sandy ford.
text: It was recorded in 1294 as Saundfordhull, the hill by the sandy ford. The ford carried the Roman road, Ermine Street, across a brook.

head: 'Stanmore' means the stony pool.
text: It comes from Old English stān, stone, and mere, a pool; the gravel soil here is very stony. The station opened in 1932.

head: Named after Star Lane, the street beside the station.
text: The origin of the street's name is not recorded. The station opened in 2011, on a new DLR line to Stratford International.

head: 'Stepney' means the landing place of a man called Stebba.
text: It was recorded around 1000 as Stybbanhythe, with hythe meaning a landing place on the Thames. The green is the old village green of Stepney.

head: 'Stockwell' means the well or spring by a tree stump.
text: It comes from Old English stocc, a stump or post. Outside the station is the entrance to a deep-level shelter built during the Second World War.

head: 'Stoke Newington' means the new farm by the tree stumps.
text: The writer Daniel Defoe lived here, and Edgar Allan Poe went to school here as a boy.

head: Named after a stone bridge over the River Brent.
text: The bridge was built in the 17th century to carry Harrow Road over the river. Bakerloo trains have called here since 1917.

head: 'Stratford' means the ford on the Roman road.
text: Old English stræt, a paved Roman road, gave us the word 'street'. Here the road from London to Colchester crossed the River Lea. The area was the centre of the 2012 Olympic Games.

head: Named after Stratford's high street, the old Roman road east from London.
text: Stratford means the ford on the Roman road, where it crossed the River Lea. The station stands on the site of the old Stratford Market station.

head: Named for the international trains that were meant to stop here.
text: The main line station opened in 2009 for trains through the Channel Tunnel, but Eurostar trains have never called here.

head: 'Sudbury' means the southern manor.
text: It was south of Harrow, the main village. The station opened in 1903; its present building is by Charles Holden, from the early 1930s.

head: 'Sudbury' means the southern manor.
text: It lay south of Harrow. The station was rebuilt in 1931 by Charles Holden as a brick and glass box, a model for many later Underground stations.

head: Named after the Surrey Commercial Docks, on the Surrey bank of the Thames.
text: The docks handled timber and grain. Greenland Dock, the oldest part, once served whaling ships. The station was called Surrey Docks until 1989.

head: Named after a pub built to look like a Swiss chalet.
text: An inn has stood on this site since the early 19th century. The pub, Ye Olde Swiss Cottage, still stands near the station.

head: 'Sydenham' started as Chipenham, the homestead of a man called Cippa.
text: It was recorded in 1206 as Chipeham. The spelling changed over the centuries, probably through a misreading, until it became Sydenham.

head: 'Taplow' means the burial mound of a man called Tæppa.
text: His mound still stands in the old churchyard. When it was dug up in 1883 it held rich Anglo-Saxon treasures, now in the British Museum.

head: Named after the Temple, once the home of the Knights Templar.
text: The knights built the round Temple Church in the 12th century. After the order was closed down in the 14th century, lawyers moved in, and the Inner and Middle Temple are still two of the Inns of Court.

head: Named after Theobalds, a great palace that belonged to William Cecil, Lord Burghley.
text: King James I loved the house so much that he swapped it for another palace, and he died there in 1625. Only fragments remain.

head: 'Bois' is the family name of medieval landowners.
text: The Bois family held the land in the 12th and 13th centuries. 'Theydon' is thought to mean the valley where thatch was gathered. The station opened in 1865 as Theydon.

head: 'Bec' recalls the Abbey of Bec in Normandy, which owned land here after 1066.
text: Tooting probably means the people of a man called Tota. The station opened in 1926 as Trinity Road (Tooting Bec) and was renamed in 1950.

head: 'Tooting' probably means the people of a man called Tota.
text: A 'broadway' is a wide main street. The statue of King Edward VII outside the station has stood there since 1911.

head: Named after the road to the manor of Tottenhall, not Tottenham.
text: The manor house, near today's Euston Road, was probably named after a landowner called Tota. The road led there from the West End.

head: 'Tottenham' means the homestead of a man called Totta.
text: 'Hale' is said to come from an old word meaning to hoist or haul: goods such as timber were unloaded from the River Lea here. The station opened with the Victoria line in 1968.

head: 'Totteridge' means the ridge of a man called Tata; 'Whetstone' is a puzzle.
text: Legend says soldiers sharpened their swords on a whetstone here before the Battle of Barnet in 1471, but the name is older than that. It more probably means 'west town'.

head: Named as a gateway to the Tower of London, which stands nearby.
text: It was the DLR's first terminus in the City when the line opened in 1987. The Tower of London was begun by William the Conqueror after 1066.

head: Named after the hill beside the Tower of London.
text: For centuries it was a place of public execution. The station was called Mark Lane until 1946.

head: Named after the Tufnell family, lords of the manor of Barnsbury.
text: William Tufnell was given the manor in 1753. His descendant Henry Tufnell began building houses on the estate in 1845. The station opened in 1907.

head: Named after Turkey Street, near the Turkey Brook in Enfield.
text: The origin of the name is uncertain; it has nothing to do with the bird or the country, as far as anyone knows.

head: 'Turnham' means the homestead in the river bend.
text: The Thames makes a large loop here. In 1642, during the Civil War, a royalist army turned back at Turnham Green instead of marching on London.

head: Named after a turnpike, a toll gate on the road north.
text: Travellers on Green Lanes had to pay here to use the road. The station opened in 1932.

head: 'Twyford' means the double ford.
text: There were two fords across the River Loddon here. Many English villages share the name for the same reason.

head: 'Upminster' means the minster, or large church, on higher ground.
text: The church was probably St Laurence, on the hill above the River Ingrebourne. Upminster's windmill, built in 1803, still stands. The station is the eastern end of the District line.

head: Named after the bridge over the River Ingrebourne, near Upminster.
text: Upminster means the large church on higher ground. The station opened in 1934.

head: 'Upney' probably means the higher island.
text: The 'island' was a patch of dry land among the streams and marshes near the Mayes Brook. The station opened in 1932.

head: 'Holloway' means the hollow way, a road worn deep into the ground.
text: Cattle and carts on their way to London's markets wore the road down over centuries.

head: 'Upton' means the farm on higher ground.
text: 'Park' was added in the 1880s to sell new houses. West Ham United's old stadium, the Boleyn Ground, was often called Upton Park.

head: 'Uxbridge' means the bridge of the Wixan people.
text: The Wixan were an Anglo-Saxon tribe who settled here, and the bridge crossed the River Colne. Uxbridge is the western end of the Metropolitan and Piccadilly lines.
